Daily pattern and comfort

Source: vignettes/daily-pattern.Rmd
daily-pattern.Rmd

The Daily Pattern and Comfort tabs of the golemenviro app draw the hourly averages of the sensors. In R, get_hourly() downloads them, plot_daily_pattern() and plot_average_day() show what repeats every day, and plot_comfort() and comfort_summary() how comfortable the room was. Gauges and time series shows how to install the package and which servers it reads.

library(golemenviro)
Sys.setenv(TZ = "Europe/Bucharest")
url <- "http://pip1.crabdance.com:1507/api/v1/query_range"

The hours are those of the time zone of the R session, here the one of the app, as Gauges and time series explains. The axis titles name it.

Download the hourly averages

get_hourly() downloads the average of each clock hour of one sensor over the last days days, 30 by default, up to the start of the current hour. It takes the name of the sensor in Prometheus, such as "temperature" or "PM25", not the name of its column in get_data(). The names of metric_mid list them all:

names(metric_mid)
#>  [1] "temperature" "humidity"    "pressure"    "lux"         "proximity"   "NH3"         "reducing"    "oxidising"   "PM1"         "PM25"        "PM10"
temperature <- get_hourly(url, "temperature", days = 30)
head(temperature)
#>         date hour    value
#> 1 2026-10-22   17 30.00611
#> 2 2026-10-22   18 29.82130
#> 3 2026-10-22   19 29.37329
#> 4 2026-10-22   20 29.99080
#> 5 2026-10-22   21 30.08549
#> 6 2026-10-22   22 30.22740

It has a row per hour: its date, its hour from 0 to 23 and the average value. When the server cannot be reached, get_hourly() returns NULL with a message. When the server has no readings of the sensor in that time, it returns a data frame without rows. The charts below take any data frame with these three columns.

Heatmap

plot_daily_pattern() draws a column per day and a row per hour, midnight at the top, each colored by the average of that hour. What happens at the same time every day shows as a horizontal band. variable names the sensor in the title and the hover labels, and unit is the unit of the readings:

plot_daily_pattern(temperature, "Temperature", degrees_celsius)

The colors run from light blue for low values to dark blue for high ones, the five steps of blue_steps. They stop at the 2nd and 98th percentiles, so that a few spikes do not wash out the rest. Hover over a cell for its exact value.

mid colors one value white, lower values blue and higher values red, and makes the colors symmetric around it. metric_mid holds the values the app uses: room temperature, the middle of the comfortable humidity, the standard air pressure at sea level, and for PM2.5 and PM10 the guidelines of the World Health Organization for a day. It is NA for the sensors with no such value, which keep the blue scale:

metric_mid
#> temperature    humidity    pressure         lux   proximity         NH3    reducing   oxidising         PM1        PM25        PM10 
#>       24.00       50.00     1013.25          NA          NA          NA          NA          NA          NA       15.00       45.00
plot_daily_pattern(temperature, "Temperature", degrees_celsius,
  mid = metric_mid[["temperature"]])

red_steps has five reds with the same lightness as the blues, for color scales of your own where higher means hotter or worse.

A typical day

plot_average_day() sums up the same hourly averages in one day. For each hour it draws the median over all the days (the line) and the middle half of the days, between the 25th and 75th percentiles (the band). A narrow band means that hour is much the same every day:

plot_average_day(temperature, "Temperature", degrees_celsius)

Comfort

plot_comfort() takes the hourly averages of temperature and humidity and draws a point for every hour that has both, at its temperature and humidity. The points are colored by the hour of the day: blue at night, orange in the morning, yellow at midday and red in the evening. The green box is the comfort zone, 20 to 25 °C and 40 to 60% humidity, and the title says how many of the hours were inside it. The corners name what lies that way:

humidity <- get_hourly(url, "humidity", days = 30)
plot_comfort(temperature, humidity)

comfort_summary() gives the numbers: how many hours had both readings, and the percentages of them that were comfortable, too warm, too cool, too dry and too humid. An hour can be both too warm and too dry:

str(comfort_summary(temperature, humidity))
#> List of 6
#>  $ hours      : int 720
#>  $ comfortable: num 1.94
#>  $ too_warm   : num 89.7
#>  $ too_cool   : num 0
#>  $ too_dry    : num 25.8
#>  $ too_humid  : num 0

Both functions take other comfortable ranges with temperature_range and humidity_range.

Dark mode

plot_daily_pattern(), plot_average_day() and plot_comfort() take mode = "dark" for a page with a dark background. It changes the colors that the functions choose. Without mid, the blue scale of the heatmap runs the other way, so that low values fade into the dark page and high values stand out. The lines, bands, points and labels are lighter.

The background stays white and the text of the axes dark: the app darkens them with its stylesheet. On a page of your own, set them with plotly::layout(). On this light page the dark colors would not read well, so the code is not run here:

plot_comfort(temperature, humidity, mode = "dark") |>
  plotly::layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#222222", plot_bgcolor = "#222222",
    font = list(color = "#dddddd")
  )

The charts are plotly objects, so htmlwidgets::saveWidget() saves any of them as a web page, as Gauges and time series shows.
